title: Dholavira built reservoirs into its city plan
body: The Harappan city of Dholavira in Gujarat stood on an island in the dry Rann of Kutch. Excavations found reservoirs, drains and dams that worked together to collect and store water.
takeaway: A city can make a short rainy season useful for much longer by deciding where the runoff should go.
visual: the stone steps and deep walls of a reservoir at Dholavira

title: Singapore made treated wastewater a national water source
body: Singapore commissioned its first NEWater factories in 2003. At the plants, used water that has already been treated is purified further, including by forcing it through membranes in a process called reverse osmosis.
takeaway: Reusing water gives a dense city a source it can keep drawing on after water goes down the drain.
source: PUB, Singapore's National Water Agency, NEWater Quality
visual: rows of membrane tubes and pipes inside a Singapore water reclamation plant

title: China joined centuries of canal works into one network
body: Parts of China's Grand Canal date back to the fifth century BCE. The Sui dynasty first unified the system in the seventh century CE. At its peak under the Yuan dynasty, it included more than 2,000 km of artificial waterways.
takeaway: The connections between old canals made it possible to move freight much farther by water.
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, The Grand Canal (2014)
visual: a freight barge on the Grand Canal between long stone embankments
